A few words to know

classification
A label used to place something in a group.
correspondence
Letters or messages exchanged.
undeliverable
Unable to reach its intended address.
effective
Working in practice, not only in theory.
context
Information needed to understand something fairly.
filing scheme
A system for arranging records.

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The newspaper archivist's next message brought a modest development. A fresh check of the surviving October 2011 subject index had identified three entries concerning the trust's student travel programme, including the item dated 12 October and labelled “decision not received”. Staff could provide dates and general headings, but access to the original correspondence remained restricted.

Emma copied the descriptions exactly. The other two entries concerned selection questions and a request for information. All three titles had been assigned by newspaper staff. They could not be treated as quotations from the authors, or even as proof that the writers had complained.

Sarah rang almost immediately.

“Three letters from unhappy families.”

“Possibly,” Emma said. “But three entries aren't necessarily three letters from three families. One writer might appear twice, and the index may not be complete.”

Sarah accepted the correction. Emma added a note beside each entry: Author unknown; content unavailable; classification editorial.

Fiona Bell's reply arrived in the afternoon. The trust's records team had not located a completed contact-attempt form. A further page from the office guidance instructed staff to record post returned as undeliverable. Yet Fiona could not verify that the rule had been followed in every case. She also confirmed that the appeals folder had not been inspected.

Emma considered what the paperwork allowed her to say. The trust had designed a process for recording outgoing notices and handling returned letters. The index suggested that correspondence about the travel scheme had reached the newspaper. Neither fact established that an unsuccessful applicant had been denied an effective opportunity to request a review.

She returned to her notes from the 18 September 2011 interview with Claire. Claire's concern had been about promises to students and what actually happened to them. Emma now wondered whether her younger self had reduced that concern to a personal dispute because it made a simpler article. Her past mistake did not make the present allegations true. It merely gave her a reason to be more exacting.

She drew four columns: Prepared, Sent, Received and Understood. A model letter addressed the first; a ledger entry could support the second. Evidence of the last two was still missing. Even proof that a decision arrived would not necessarily show that the applicant knew how to challenge it within fourteen days.

When Sarah asked whether they had enough to publish, Emma distinguished a report on the documented procedures from an accusation about individual harm. The former might be possible with proper context. The latter was not supported.

Then she noticed something in the archive's reply: the three subject entries came from different sections of the index. She had mentally grouped them because they concerned the same programme, but the filing scheme itself might explain why their headings differed.

She wrote to the archivist asking how the sections had been organised. Before drawing connections among three uncertain entries, she wanted to know whether the archive had intended them to be connected at all.
